rows.subtype: Approach: rebuild a schedule after a salary change [Revision]
rows.description: After a raise, the borrower recalculates the payoff date in a spreadsheet, increases the EMI slightly and sets a reminder to review every six months. Small planned revisions keep the loan on track.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: avoidance and procrastination, pre-mortem, prioritising, pros and cons, resource and budget planning, working backward

rows.description: The borrower imagines defaulting in year two and lists causes such as job loss or a medical bill, then keeps a small reserve and a note of who to call at the bank. Foreseeing failure builds a cushion.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: avoidance and procrastination, prioritising, pros and cons, resource and budget planning, working backward

rows.subtype: Approach: set up auto-debit with a reminder [Action]
rows.description: The graduate links the EMI to auto-debit a day after salary credit and sets a balance alert. Automation avoids forgetting due dates, though the balance still needs watching.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: pre-mortem, prioritising, pros and cons, resource and budget planning, working backward

rows.subtype: Approach: inversion asking how the offer could be a trap [Thinking]
rows.description: A student offered a promised monthly return of 10 percent by a college senior asks what would have to be true for that to be real, and sees that no lawful investment guarantees it. Imagining the trap first reveals warning signs.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: cutting losses, impulsive action

rows.subtype: Approach: check registration with the regulator before paying [Action]
rows.description: Before sending money, the person looks up whether the platform and the adviser are registered with SEBI or the relevant regulator, and reads reviews and complaints. A few minutes of checking replaces trust in a persuasive pitch.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: cutting losses, impulsive action, inversion

rows.subtype: Approach: fear of missing out drives a quick decision [Pitfall]
rows.description: Seeing friends post screenshots of gains, a young worker rushes into a Telegram tip group and transfers savings within an hour. Social proof and urgency shut down checking, and the money cannot be recovered.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: cutting losses, inversion

rows.subtype: Approach: slow down and sleep on any pressured offer [Thinking]
rows.description: The person adopts a rule of waiting 48 hours before any money moves for an investment. Time reduces the pull of urgency, and a genuine opportunity would still be there after the wait.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: cutting losses, impulsive action, inversion

rows.subtype: Approach: consult a trusted family member or a registered adviser [Action]
rows.description: The student shows the offer to an uncle who works in a bank and to a registered adviser. Both point out unrealistic returns and the absence of paperwork, and the student declines with confidence.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: cutting losses, impulsive action, inversion

rows.subtype: Approach: small test amount that grows into a big commitment [Pitfall]
rows.description: A first small payout from a fake app builds trust, so the person invests a larger sum and recruits friends. The early gain was bait, and the pattern of sunk cost keeps the person paying.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: impulsive action, inversion

rows.subtype: Approach: report and stop after noticing withdrawal blocks [Revision]
rows.description: When the app asks for a further fee to release money, the person sees the pattern, stops paying, saves the chats and screenshots, and files a complaint on the cybercrime portal and with the bank. Cutting losses early limits harm.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: impulsive action, inversion
